one_liner: Portable scalar 64/128-bit C hash; beats XXH3-64 by about 1.35x on 1 MiB bulk in SIMD-less wasm32.
what_it_does: hayahash is a single-header C (static inline) non-cryptographic hash with one-shot hayahash64(buf, len, seed) and hayahash128(buf, len, seed), plus a streaming init/update/digest API. One streaming state serves both widths, and the 128-bit low word always equals hayahash64. Bit-exact ports exist for Rust, Go, Zig, Java, C#, Python, Swift, JS/TS (wasm with a pure-JS fallback), Haskell and MIPS64, giving the same digest on every language and byte order. It has the same (bytes, length, 64-bit seed) shape as XXH3_64bits_withSeed, but the names and digest values differ, and pre-1.0 digests may still change.
how_it_is_fast: It uses only 64-bit multiplication mod 2^64: no 64x64->128 multiply, no SIMD and no AES, which is all that baseline wasm32 provides. XXH3 and rapidhash must emulate wide multiplication there. Inputs of 320 bytes or more run 8 independent lanes over 64-byte blocks, where each absorb is h = (h ^ (w + rotl(prev_w, 27))) * K, so the loop-carried chain is only add->mul. The 8 lanes then fold into 4, the tail uses overlapping wyhash-style reads, and inputs of 16 bytes or less take a dedicated two-multiply path. On Zen 4/5 with AVX-512DQ, GCC auto-vectorizes the bulk loop.
when_to_use: Hashing inside WebAssembly without SIMD (browser or Node wasm32): at 1 MiB it measured 23.55 GB/s vs 17.41 for XXH3-64 and 14.71 for XXH64 on an M1 Pro under V8, and from 32-byte keys up it also had lower chained latency than both.
Systems that must compute the same digest in several languages or byte orders (for example a Go or Rust server and a browser client), with everyone pinned to the same hayahash version.
Chunked or streaming input where you want both a 64-bit and a 128-bit digest from one pass; on bulk input the 128-bit result costs only an extra finalizer (23.34 vs 23.55 GB/s in wasm).
Targets without a fast 64x64->128 multiply (wasm32, 32-bit or exotic CPUs, MIPS64), where wide-multiply hashes fall back to emulation.
when_not_to_use: Native x86-64/AArch64 builds where XXH3 is available: the author makes no native 64-bit competitive claim, and in the SMHasher3 128-bit shootout XXH3-128 has higher bulk throughput (12.64 vs 9.77 B/cycle on M1, 48.91 vs 31.02 on Zen 5).
Latency-critical keys of 4-16 bytes in wasm: XXH64 was faster at 4-8 bytes (5.9-6.0 vs 7.6-7.7 ns chained) and tied at 16 bytes.
Anything that persists digests (on-disk indexes, wire formats, caches shared across deploys): digests changed in 0.3.0 and 0.5.0 (2026-08-09) and can change again before 1.0.
Adversarial inputs or authentication: it is explicitly non-cryptographic, a secret seed only reduces HashDoS risk, and the design notes do not prove collision resistance for the full hash.
Teams that need a proven dependency: the repo is about two months old with 2 stars, a single maintainer and no externally filed issues.

integration.min_toolchain: C11 as built in CI; also compiled as C++11 and C++17 with g++ and clang++, and MSVC x64 is conformance-tested. Ports: Zig 0.16, Java 17+, .NET 8+, CPython 3.9+, Swift 5.9+, GHC 8.10+
integration.platforms: any (portable scalar code); CI covers x86-64, AArch64, big-endian s390x, wasm32, MSVC x64 and MIPS64 n64
integration.thread_safety: Not documented; one-shot functions are static inline with no global state, and the streaming state is a caller-owned struct
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial — the call shape (pointer, length, 64-bit seed) matches XXH3_64bits_withSeed/XXH64, but the function names, digest values and length type (signed ptrdiff_t) differ, so a thin wrapper is needed and stored hashes must be recomputed

gotchas: len is a signed ptrdiff_t and must be non-negative; the pointer may be null only when len is 0.
hayahash128(...).lo is exactly hayahash64(...). Do not treat a 64-bit and a 128-bit digest of the same data as independent bits.
The streaming state is about 544 bytes (a 448-byte buffer plus lane words). Totals under 448 bytes stay buffered and go through the one-shot path when you call digest.

Speed depends on per-compiler dispatch shapes: GCC length tiers, Zen 4/5-only AVX-512DQ vectorization (without it Zen 5 bulk drops from about 61.6 to about 35 GB/s), and clang asm barriers. MSVC performance is untested. The wasm harness drops xxHash from -msimd128 builds, so there is no comparison against SIMD XXH3 in wasm.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Over xxHash (XXH3-64/XXH64), pick it when the code runs as SIMD-less wasm32 or on hardware without wide multiply and keys are 32 bytes or more; natively, or for 4-16-byte keys, stay with xxHash. Over ChibiHash, which is in the same portable ordinary-multiply class, it was faster than ChibiHash v2 at every measured size on M1 and in wasm. Over haya32x64 by the same author, pick it when you are hashing bulk data through wasm or native code rather than tiny keys in pure JS.
verified_claims_summary: One baseline wasm32 module (zig cc 0.16.0 -O3, no SIMD or wide-multiply instructions) was run under Node 26.7.0 / V8 14.6 on a bare-metal Apple M1 Pro, with timing loops inside wasm. At 1 MiB it measured hayahash64 23.55 GB/s and hayahash128 23.34, vs XXH3-64 17.41 and XXH64 14.71 (about 1.35x and 1.60x); XXH64 kept the lowest 4-8-byte chained latency. xxHash and rapidhash sources were pinned to upstream commits, and there is a single host and a single run record dated 2026-08-09.
status_note: Actively developed by one author (v0.6.0 on 2026-09-13, several fixes committed 2026-09-26), Unlicense and one copyable header. It is still pre-1.0 with unstable digests and little outside use: 2 stars, about 250 crates.io downloads, about 290 npm downloads in the last month.
